title: Pawn promotion: the pawn that becomes a queen
description: A pawn that crosses the whole board earns an extraordinary reward: it must become a queen, rook, bishop or knight. Why promotion exists, and why almost everyone chooses the queen.

body.heading: The long walk pays off
paragraphs: A pawn that reaches the far end of the board — the eighth rank for White, the first for Black — cannot stay a pawn. In the same move it must be replaced by a queen, rook, bishop or knight of its own colour. It can never become a king, and it cannot refuse the upgrade.

Promotion is why a single passed pawn can decide a game. A player who is a whole rook down can still win by shepherding one pawn to the end, because the new queen is worth more than the piece they lost.

body.heading: Why the queen, almost always
paragraphs: Queening is the default because the queen is the strongest piece, combining rook and bishop moves. Players occasionally choose a knight instead — underpromotion — when the knight's jump gives an immediate check the queen could not, or when queening would stalemate the opponent.
You may promote to a piece you still have on the board, so two queens at once is perfectly legal. In practice the spare queen is often shown with an upside-down rook.

takeaway: A pawn that reaches the far rank must promote — usually to a queen, which is why one small pawn can outweigh a lost rook.
